title: Emversity raises $30M Series A led by Premji Invest, valued at $120M
excerpt: Emversity raised a $30M Series A led by Premji Invest at a reported $120M valuation. How its university skilling model works, fees and plans.
content:
Bengaluru-based Emversity, which trains university students for jobs in healthcare and hospitality, raised a $30 million (₹271 crore) Series A in January 2026 led by Premji Invest, with Lightspeed and Z47 also investing, according to Z47's announcement. The round valued the company at about $120 million after the money, double its valuation in April 2025, TechCrunch reported, citing sources.

Emversity was started in 2023 by Vivek Sinha, a former chief operating officer of Unacademy. It works inside existing universities, adding job-focused training to degree programmes for roles such as nurse, physiotherapist, lab technician and hotel staff. This article covers the round, how the model works, what the company has disclosed since, and the open questions.

Key takeaways

  • Premji Invest led a $30 million Series A, taking Emversity's total funding to $46 million.
  • TechCrunch reported a post-money valuation of about $120 million, up from about $60 million in April 2025.
  • At the time of the round, Emversity worked with 23 universities across 40 campuses and had trained about 4,500 learners and placed 800, according to TechCrunch.
  • It plans to reach 200 campuses and add engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) and manufacturing training.
  • In March 2026, it bought back ₹6.5 crore of employee stock options from 20 early staff, according to Inc42.

The round

The Series A was announced on 14 and 15 January 2026. Premji Invest led it, advised by law firm Khaitan & Co, which handled due diligence and the deal documents. Existing investors Lightspeed and Z47, the firm formerly called Matrix Partners India, also took part, according to Entrackr.

It was Emversity's third round in under two years. According to Entrackr:

  • Seed, April 2024: $11 million led by Matrix Partners India (now Z47) and Lightspeed.
  • Pre-Series A: $5 million led by Lightspeed and Z47, with Alteria Capital and InnoVen Capital.
  • Series A, January 2026: $30 million led by Premji Invest.

That adds up to the $46 million total that Emversity and its investors have cited.

What the investors said

Kaveesh Chawla of Premji Invest said Emversity's "student-centric approach" and links with industry partners put it in a good position to close the gap between education and jobs, according to Z47. Harsha Kumar of Lightspeed called it "a disciplined, outcomes-led platform". Sinha said India had added a lot of higher-education capacity over the past decade, but the link between education and employability had not kept pace.

How Emversity's model works

Emversity does not run its own university. It partners with existing universities to embed industry-designed courses, work-integrated training and technology into their degree programmes, according to Z47. It also runs its own skill centres for shorter certificate courses. TechCrunch reported that in 2025, revenue was split roughly evenly between university programmes and skill-centre certifications.

The company focuses on what TechCrunch called "grey-collar" jobs: skilled, hands-on roles that are hard to automate. Sinha's example was intensive care, where a hospital needs a nurse for every two ICU beds regardless of how much paperwork AI takes over.

Employers help design the training and hire graduates. Z47's announcement listed Fortis Healthcare, Apollo Hospitals, Aster and KIMS in healthcare, and IHCL (the Taj group) and Lemon Tree Hotels in hospitality.

Programmes and fees

Emversity's website, checked on 4 October 2026, lists three main tracks. Fees and salary ranges are the company's own figures; it says salaries are indicative and set by employers, and placements are not guaranteed.

TrackWhat it isDurationTotal feeStated salary range
SPRINTNSDC-certified skill course (for example, emergency medical technician or phlebotomy) at Emversity centres1 year₹0.8 lakh to ₹1.8 lakh₹20,000 to ₹35,000 a month
EDGEFour-year degree awarded by a partner university, with 18 healthcare specialisations4 years₹7.2 lakh₹25,000 to ₹50,000 a month
GATEWAYHospitality diploma with training in Goa and 12 months abroad24 months₹5 lakh₹1 lakh to ₹1.2 lakh a month

For readers outside India: 1 lakh is 100,000 rupees and 1 crore is 10 million. NSDC is the National Skill Development Corporation, which certifies vocational courses.

The numbers Emversity has disclosed

Emversity is private and has disclosed only selected figures. At the time of the round, TechCrunch reported:

  • 23 partner universities and more than 40 campus locations;
  • about 4,500 learners trained and 800 placed;
  • about 700 employees, including 200 to 250 trainers;
  • gross margins of about 80%, with customer acquisition costs below 10% of revenue; and
  • more than 350,000 enquiries in 2025 to its career-counselling platform, which contributed over 20% of revenue.

By March 2026, Inc42 reported that Emversity had more than 700 employees in 60-plus locations across 24 states. Its website now claims 30+ partner universities, 60+ locations and a 98% placement rate for graduating batches. That last figure is a company claim that we could not independently verify. Emversity has not published audited revenue or profit figures in the sources we reviewed, so we do not report any.

Where the money goes

According to Z47 and Entrackr, Emversity plans to:

  • expand from about 40 campuses to more than 200, which TechCrunch reported as a two-year goal;
  • deepen its healthcare and hospitality programmes;
  • add new verticals in EPC and manufacturing; and
  • strengthen its technology platform.

Inc42's March report described a larger ambition of 400 campuses over two and a half years. The company is also looking at placing Indian-trained healthcare workers abroad, in countries with ageing populations such as Japan and Germany, though it gave TechCrunch no timeline. Its website already markets an international hospitality track and lists healthcare salary ranges for Germany and the US.

The ESOP buyback

Two months after the round, Emversity bought back ₹6.5 crore of vested employee stock options from 20 employees, according to Inc42. Staff who joined on or before 31 January 2024 could sell up to 70% of their vested options at the current valuation, without a discount. Chief human resources officer Megha Lal said the company preferred to reward early employees now rather than wait for a secondary sale or IPO that might be years away.

This is an early buyback for a company founded in 2023. It suggests the Series A left Emversity with enough cash to spare some for staff liquidity, and it is a useful signal for job seekers weighing equity offers from young startups.

The policy tailwind

Emversity's chosen sectors line up with government priorities. India's Union Budget 2026-27, presented on 1 February 2026, proposed upgrading existing allied health professional (AHP) institutions, setting up new ones in the private and government sectors, and adding 100,000 allied health professionals over five years, according to the Press Information Bureau. The budget also proposed a high-powered "Education to Employment and Enterprise" standing committee and upgrading the National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology into a National Institute of Hospitality.

Allied health professionals include radiology, operation-theatre and lab technicians, the roles Emversity trains for. A public push to expand AHP training could bring both more demand for such courses and more competition from public and private institutions.

Why it matters

Emversity's round shows where education investors are putting money in 2026: into models tied to specific jobs and employers, rather than open-ended online courses. Its pitch rests on outcomes, so the numbers that matter most are placement rates, starting salaries and how many students complete programmes, and so far these come mainly from the company itself.

For founders, the lesson is in the distribution. By working through existing universities, Emversity avoids building campuses and uses the universities' degree-granting status, while selling employers a supply of trained staff. The risks are execution across hundreds of campuses, the quality of training at that scale, and student fees in a market where entry-level salaries can be ₹20,000 to ₹35,000 a month by the company's own figures.

Follow more edtech and other rounds on our funding tracker, and see current openings on our jobs board. Students considering any paid programme should check fees, accreditation and placement terms directly with the institution.

FAQ

How much did Emversity raise in its Series A?

$30 million (₹271 crore) in January 2026, led by Premji Invest with Lightspeed and Z47. Total funding is $46 million.

What is Emversity's valuation?

About $120 million post-money after the Series A, up from about $60 million in April 2025, according to TechCrunch, citing sources.

Who founded Emversity?

Vivek Sinha, a former chief operating officer of Unacademy, founded it in 2023. It is run by Beyond Odds Technologies.

What courses does Emversity offer?

Healthcare and hospitality training, from one-year NSDC certificate courses to four-year partner-university degrees and an international hospitality diploma.

How many campuses does Emversity have?

About 40 at the time of the Series A, and 60+ locations by its own later count. It plans to reach 200 or more.

Is Emversity a university?

No. Degrees are awarded by its partner universities. Emversity provides the industry training, curriculum and placement support.
